items.q: Everyone says smaller apps convert better. What actually moves install conversion?
shortAnswer: Size moves conversion mainly in low-storage and metered markets — but store listing, ratings, and perceived quality move installs at least as much.
The cheapest lever is the AAB split (30-50% smaller downloads); asset packs and dynamic features only pay off when shedding genuinely optional, large assets.
Measure conversion with Play Console experiments — if a size change doesn't move the funnel, don't spend engineering time on the next 10 MB.
items.answer:
#### What the data actually says
Download size correlates with conversion in emerging, low-storage, and metered-data markets — the user watches the progress bar, and a large download plus a slow cold start is a drop-off. In mature markets a 10 MB shave moves little; ratings, screenshots, and description decide the click. The rational position: **optimize size where the funnel shows it matters**, not because "smaller is better" is a slogan.
#### The lever ordering
1. **AAB with full splits** — the largest guaranteed saving (30–50% smaller installs) at near-zero engineering cost.
2. **R8 plus resource shrinking** — removes what you don't ship at all.
3. **Asset packs** — move big, optional assets (video, level data, offline maps) out of the install: install-time, fast-follow shortly after install, or on-demand delivery.
4. **Dynamic feature modules** — rarely used features installed on demand, at the cost of delivery complexity: a module per feature, versioning, and module states to manage.
#### The trap
Teams optimize size with no conversion signal. The professional version runs the funnel as an experiment — ship a smaller variant, measure installs and first-run behavior, and only invest in asset packs when the delta justifies the complexity they add. Also count the non-install cost: a 500 MB app with an aggressive on-demand scheme can convert worse than a 60 MB one that just works.
